title: Field cheat sheet: inference service comparison for engineering buyers
content:
Purpose: quick-reference sheet for AE/SE when talking to platform or SRE buyers who are evaluating hosted/managed endpoints from hyperscalers (AWS/GCP/Azure) vs Redwood. Target audience: infra/platform engineering, SRE, ML infra leads.

High-level framing (one-liner to lead with):
- Hyperscalers sell convenience at scale, but platform teams care about operational predictability, control surface, and the ability to recover and iterate without vendor lock or surprise costs. Redwood is built for operational ownership: predictable SLOs, transparent unit economics, and staged migration paths that de-risk production LLM features.

Top-level win themes (speak in orders of priority for engineering buyers):
1) Deterministic economics and observability
  - Hyperscalers: opaque token/unit pricing across tiers, meter variability; hard to attribute cost to product features.
  - Redwood: token-level cost traces, per-route histograms, and tooling to model cost at feature-level before launch.
  - Quick line: "We make it easy to forecast cost per feature and set automated throttles before your first spike."

2) Failure modes & graceful degradation
  - Hyperscalers: single-plane managed endpoints can be opaque about throttling/backpressure behavior and fallback chains.
  - Redwood: explicit fallback policies, canary rollouts to cheaper model variants, and region/pool routing policies so you maintain a user experience even under provider pressure.
  - Demo hook: show a canary rollback from a heavy model to a distilled quantized variant in < 60s.

3) Deployment parity and portability
  - Hyperscalers: often tempting to embed deep into a cloud account; migration to another provider or on-prem is painful.
  - Redwood: identical API, config, and rollout semantics across hosted/dedicated/private, designed for staged migration.
  - Objection-handling: "We can't lift-and-shift easily" -> "We have a migration playbook and config comparison tool; typical migration is layered (ingress, model, rollout), not forklift."

4) SRE-friendly controls and SLAs
  - Hyperscalers: SLAs exist but the practical SLOs teams need (p95 token latency for mixed workloads, tail isolation) are hard to validate.
  - Redwood: token-level latency breakdowns, per-model pX tracking, and route-level autoscaling knobs that SREs can map into existing on-call runbooks.
  - Talking point: "You can pin latency SLOs to feature routes and tie alerting directly to customer-impacting metrics."

5) Regulatory/air-gap readiness (for finance/healthcare customers)
  - Hyperscalers: fine for many, but not always acceptable for regulated workloads.
  - Redwood: private control plane and on-prem packages with KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs.

Practical comparison bullets (short punchy lines to read aloud):
- Cost shocks: hyperscalers -> possible under load. Redwood -> predictable reserved pools + burst policy.
- Debugging: hyperscalers -> limited token-level traces. Redwood -> full token and KV cache traces for repro.
- Model upgrades: hyperscalers -> opaque staging; Redwood -> canary/A-B with deterministic fallback.
- Vendor dependency: hyperscalers -> deeper coupling to cloud infra. Redwood -> deployment abstraction across environments.

SRE playbook snippets (for customer conversations)
- If customer asks about an outage: walk through Redwood's multi-tier fallback (model variant -> local cache -> lightweight embed-only route) and show how traffic can be routed to a cheaper pool while preserving a soft-failure UX.
- If customer asks about burst cost controls: explain reserved capacity + burst governance policies and how we can limit per-API-key QPS and enforce queue depth thresholds.
- If customer asks about debugging memory leaks or token explosion: demonstrate our KV cache visualization and per-request token trace that maps to serving kernels.

Demo checklist (quick steps for an SE-run demo):
1) Prep two model variants: base large model and quantized small variant (same behavior on prompt set).
2) Create a route with canary allocation 10% -> 90% then trigger a synthetic latency spike.
3) Show Redwood console: route metrics, token-level latency heatmap, and trigger automated rollback.
4) Flip to private deployment slide: show identical API call that hits private control plane (emphasize parity).
5) End with a cost forecast: projected cost delta for 1M requests/month under mixed-length tokens.

Objections and short rebuttals (two-liners):
- "Hyperscaler gives us one bill, easier ops." -> "True — they manage infra, but that convenience often hides variability. We give you predictable bills and tools to tie spend to product metrics. Teams that need predictability choose reserved pools + observability.\n- "We already have credits/negotiated pricing with cloud." -> "We integrate into your cloud billing surface where needed, but our reserved/dedicated options are priced to beat surprise overages and simplify forecasting."\n- "Migration is too expensive." -> "We recommend a staged migration: start with the non-critical surface (batch or low-traffic feature), validate, then roll core flows. Typical pilot is 2–6 weeks."

Suggested field-friendly email opener (short):
- "Quick note — platform teams we speak with are less concerned about peak TPS and more about unclear tail behavior and surprise spend during traffic spikes. Can we run a 2-week pilot to validate tail latency and cost for one feature?"

Notes-to-self / follow-ups (for AE/SE):
- Bring sample token-level cost graph for customers with >5M tokens/month.
- Add one-pager comparing our reserved capacity SLAs vs common hyperscaler endpoint expectations.
- Record a 4-min demo clip of canary rollback to include in SDR outreach.

Short checklist for qualification call (yes/no):
- Do they track per-feature cost today? (Y/N)
- Are they comfortable with a single cloud lock-in? (Y/N)
- Do they need private deployment / KMS? (Y/N)
- Are tail latencies a blocker for shipping? (Y/N)

Appendix (quick facts to memorize):
- Typical migration pilot length: 2–6 weeks.
- Common hyperscaler pain: opaque throttling behavior, surprise quotas during scale tests.
- Redwood differentiator shorthand: "Predictable economics + ops-first fallbacks + environment parity."

References / links to hand off post-call:
- Migration playbook (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/OPS/migration-playbook
- Demo repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/demo-scripts
- Quick pricing explainer: https://redwood.ai/pricing/hosted-vs-dedicated

End of cheat sheet. Keep this short on calls — use the demo to prove the fallback story rather than long slides.

Internal revision notes: convert to a 1-pager slide for SDR/SDR+AE handoff; add two customer quotes about avoiding cost surprises.
